stages.title: From an interest to the field's own search words
goal: Turn your interest into the words the field uses
Why: you see the whole area, not your guess of it
how: Write your interest in one sentence
Split it: phenomenon · context · angle (e.g. language on signs · Islamabad · readers' views)
Add synonyms and field terms; quote phrases: "linguistic landscape"
Filter 2016–2026, Linguistics, PDF; skim the top 30 titles and abstracts
care: Thousands of results: too broad, so add context or angle
Zero results: wrong words, not a gap
Note the words good papers keep using: your next terms
leave: A keyword list: your words plus the field's words
Search log rows: date, words, filters, counts
stages.prompt: “My interest: [one sentence]. List the terms this field uses for it, with synonyms. Do not suggest a topic.”

stages.title: Measure the field before you choose a corner of it
goal: Know the size and speed of your area
Why: crowded needs a sharp angle; growing means timely but competitive; empty means check words or feasibility
how: Count papers per year for 2 or 3 phrasings
Read the sample ARS returns; mark how many are on topic
care: A count is only as good as its words: always read the sample
Zero does not mean open; Semantic Scholar's thousands are not the field
leave: One sentence on saturation, e.g. “58 papers, most since 2022, mostly sign counts”
The trend and the on-topic share
stages.prompt: “How many papers on "linguistic landscape" in Pakistan were published each year since 2016? Show me a sample and how many are on topic.”

stages.title: Read the closest studies to see what is missing
goal: Find what the closest studies did and did not do
Why: a gap comes from evidence, not from an idea
how: Pick 5 for a first look, 10 to 20 for a synopsis
Choose by: closest topic and context, last 5 years plus 2 or 3 classics, a mix of methods, peer reviewed, Pakistani and international
Upload lawful PDFs; extract per paper: context, sample, framework, method, findings, limitations, future work
care: The notebook knows only your papers: its gaps are gaps among them
Open each PDF to check what it cites
leave: A reading matrix (one row per paper)
2 or 3 gap hypotheses, each with its sources
stages.prompt: “For each paper: context, sample, framework, method, findings, limitations, future work. One table, cite every cell.” Then: “What did none of these papers do? Cite each.”

stages.title: Find your rivals, and check every reference
goal: Test each hypothesis against the whole field, not five papers
Why: if a study already answers your question, an examiner will name it
how: Search with the field's terms; include the Pakistan lane
For each rival: same question? same context? same method?
Verify every reference you will cite against Crossref
care: Search prr.hec.gov.pk: unpublished theses are not indexed
Drop retracted papers; note online-first years
leave: A rival list with links: what each did, what yours must add
stages.prompt: “Find the published studies closest to: [hypothesis]. Include Pakistani authors. Does any already answer my question?” · “Verify this reference: …”

stages.title: Test the gap from every angle, then narrow it
goal: Show the gap is real, specific and worth filling
Why: “no one has studied this” is a claim that needs evidence
how: Validate by: evidence · rivals · the field's terms · context (does Pakistan change it?) · method · significance
Narrow to one place, one group, one data type, one framework, one semester
care: Fake-gap alarms: “first in Pakistan” with nothing changed; same lens, another text; few results from the wrong words
leave: Verdict: Supported, Partly or Not yet
Evidence table, search log, what to check by hand
stages.prompt: “Use the ARS gap-finder method. My gap: [one sentence]. Build the evidence table, run the rival check and the alarms, and tell me what to check by hand.”

stages.title: Write the topic, then test it as an examiner would
goal: Turn the gap into a topic your supervisor can approve
Why: a defensible topic saves a semester
how: Topic statement: [phenomenon] in [context], through [framework], using [data and method], to find out [what is unknown], because [why it matters]
Draft 2 or 3 research questions from it
Run the 8 checks: clarity, alignment, rivals, saturation, significance, feasibility, defensibility, supervisor fit
care: Future hurdles: access to participants, ethics approval, questionnaire language, time, cost, supervisor expertise, journal fit (HJRS)
leave: Ready, Refine or Not yet, plus 3 examiner questions
Log row and carry-forward block, for your supervisor meeting
stages.prompt: “Use the ARS topic-check method. My topic: [statement]. Test it as an examiner would. Do not rewrite it.”
